kb.mission.label: Mission statement
kb.mission.text: Launchpad builds accelerated pathways that connect Philadelphia young adults to high-paying, future-ready tech careers. Through a paid AI-engineering program grounded in real client work, participants who arrive with a high school diploma and little else gain applied AI skills, industry certifications, a portfolio of deployed work, and the paid experience employers now demand — at no cost to them — on a path toward a $50,000 living wage.

kb.history.label: Org history & accomplishments
kb.history.text: Launchpad started in 2023 as an initiative of Building 21, a nonprofit that has run competency-based schools and worked with schools and districts nationally since 2013 (across 20 states, serving 10,000+ students). Launchpad designed its LiftOff track in 2022 and enrolled its first cohort in January 2023; that first LiftOff cohort of {{placement_denominator}} graduated in October 2025 at a ceremony hosted by employer partner Accenture, giving Launchpad a full multi-year cycle from enrollment through paid work and post-graduation outcomes. To date Launchpad has served about {{students_served}} students across its programs. Building 21 is the fiscal sponsor (EIN 47-2514219); Launchpad plans to spin out as its own 501(c)(3).

kb.programs.label: Current programs & core services
kb.programs.text: Launchpad runs as connected levels. (1) Launchpad Foundations — an entry summer program in core AI and technical skills. (2) Launchpad 101 — a yearlong, learn-and-earn program for high school juniors and seniors, four afternoons a week with summer intensives, where students earn stipends, complete paid internships, and earn industry certifications (e.g. Certiport Generative AI Foundations); it offers two pathways, Software Development and Entrepreneurial Leadership, so students not drawn to coding still build real AI/STEM skills. (3) LiftOff — a six-month, full-time, AI-first software-development track for graduates ready to go deeper (participants 18–24), with a guaranteed {{stipend_floor}} stipend floor over six months plus wraparound supports (transportation, food, a laptop, and coaching). (4) Launchpad Inc. — a nonprofit social enterprise, now the second half of LiftOff, that puts participants on paid client projects at {{avg_hourly_wage}} for local nonprofits, foundations, and small businesses. Participants train against Launchpad's AI Engineer competency framework — six competencies and 24 skills, staged Associate → AI Engineer (Junior is the graduation bar) — assessed on deployed work rather than seat time and tracked in Beacon, Building 21's competency and data platform.

kb.need.label: Statement of need
kb.need.text: In Philadelphia, a young person can finish high school, be genuinely capable, and still have no way into a career. Roughly 8,000 students a year graduate from the city's non-selective high schools without a clear path, and AI has made the first rung harder to reach: entry-level job postings have fallen sharply since 2023, and employers increasingly hire for demonstrated, deployed work rather than potential — exactly what a young person without a degree, an unpaid internship, or a professional network cannot assemble. Launchpad's participants are overwhelmingly Black or Brown (about {{demographics_black_brown}}), nearly all from low-income households (all qualify for free or reduced-price lunch), and most come from schools that offered no rigorous technical or AI training. A Philadelphia high school graduate with no further credential earns roughly $12,500 a year; the opportunity, and the gap Launchpad closes, is the path to a $50,000 living wage.

kb.program_desc.label: Program/project description
kb.program_desc.text: Launchpad recruits Philadelphia young people from non-selective high schools, no prior experience required, and pays them from day one so finishing is financially possible. The advanced phases most funders support are LiftOff — six months of full-time, AI-first software-development training for participants 18–24 — and Launchpad Inc., a nonprofit social enterprise that puts participants on real, paid client projects ({{avg_hourly_wage}}) building automations, dashboards, integrations, and agents for Philadelphia nonprofits and small businesses. Participants train against the AI Engineer competency framework (six competencies, 24 skills; prompting and context engineering, building automations and agents, connecting systems, structuring data, evaluating AI output, and managing cost and risk), earn industry certifications (Generative AI Foundations, PCEP), and are assessed on deployed work tracked in Beacon, so every graduate finishes with a portfolio of shipped AI systems and the client references early-career tech hiring now screens on. Wraparound supports — a guaranteed {{stipend_floor}} stipend floor, transportation, food, a laptop, and Career Success Coaching that continues through the first year of employment — remove the barriers that otherwise force low-income young adults to drop out. Delivered at no cost from Launchpad's Center City hub at 801 Market Street.

kb.target_population.label: Target population
kb.target_population.text: Launchpad serves Philadelphia young people ages 16–24: high school juniors and seniors (roughly 16–18) in Launchpad 101, and recent graduates / young adults (18–24) in LiftOff and Launchpad Inc. Participants come almost entirely from non-selective Philadelphia high schools; all qualify for free or reduced-price lunch, nearly {{demographics_low_income}} are from low-income households, and about {{demographics_black_brown}} are Black or Brown. No prior coding experience is required. (Funders that require an 18–24 band are served by the LiftOff/Inc profile; Launchpad 101 reaches the 16–18 group.)

kb.outcomes.label: Outcomes & results committed
kb.outcomes.text: Launchpad measures success as earning power over time toward a $50,000 living wage, not a job on graduation day, and tracks participants at six and twelve months. Results to date: LiftOff Cohort 1 — {{placement_denominator}} graduates (Oct 2025); at six months {{placement_numerator}} of {{placement_denominator}} ({{placement_rate_6mo}}) were in paid work or training, roughly three-quarters of it contract work through Launchpad Inc., averaging about {{earnings_6mo}} annualized at six months and projected toward {{earnings_9mo}} at nine months; {{placement_rate_now}} are in paid work now (most recent status); alumni have earned {{alumni_wages}} in documented wages. Notable placements: four graduates hired at Seer Interactive after out-competing 200+ applicants, plus roles at Bentley Systems, a Hack Club fellowship, and a promotion at CreateAccess. Since 2023, Launchpad has paid {{wages_total}} directly to {{wage_participants}} participants across {{wage_jobs}} jobs (most recent precise figure, William Penn Jul 2026). Launchpad 101: {{lp101_completion_rate}} completion in the most recent program year; {{lp101_transition_rate}} of graduates move directly into college, further training, or work; PCEP Python pass rates {{cert_pass_rate_range}} per cohort ({{cert_pass_rate_recent}} most recent). Twelve-month retention data arrives in fall 2026.

kb.evaluation.label: Evaluation methods
kb.evaluation.text: Launchpad assesses participants on deployed work against the AI Engineer competency framework (six competencies, 24 skills), with each skill evidenced by a portfolio artifact — a shipped integration, a system a client confirmed — tracked in Beacon, Building 21's competency platform, rather than by seat time or a single test. Program-level, Launchpad tracks completion and retention by cohort and phase, industry certifications earned (Generative AI Foundations, PCEP), and the headline outcome: the share of graduates in paid work or training and average annualized earnings against the $50,000 living-wage target, measured at six and twelve months. Results feed back into each cohort's design, and Launchpad reports completions, placements, placement rate at completion, and twelve-month retention to funders.

kb.sustainability.label: Sustainability & future funding
kb.sustainability.text: Launchpad is fully funded for the current year with no operating deficit, and is deliberately diversifying so grants carry less of the load over time. The FY2026 revenue mix is roughly {{revenue_share_grants}} foundation grants, {{revenue_share_individual}} individual donors, {{revenue_share_government}} government workforce funding, and {{revenue_share_corporate}} corporate, plus Pennsylvania EITC contributions (donors can claim up to a 90% state tax credit). Two newer streams are designed to reduce grant reliance: earned revenue through Launchpad Inc. (client work that, as the social enterprise matures, is intended to cover a rising share of program cost — the paid-work engine that trains participants also helps fund them), and a dual-enrollment partnership with Mastery Charter School that brings per-student public funding tied to enrollment rather than the grant cycle. Building 21 provides finance, compliance, and back-office infrastructure as fiscal sponsor. Anchor philanthropic support has included a {{wpf_grant_total}} three-year William Penn Foundation grant (announced 2023, following an initial {{wpf_initial_grant}}).

kb.uniqueness.label: What makes LaunchPad unique
kb.uniqueness.text: Three things set Launchpad apart. First, participants are paid from day one — a guaranteed {{stipend_floor}} stipend floor plus paid client work at {{avg_hourly_wage}} — so low-income young adults can finish full-time training instead of taking immediate work; the financial barrier that ends most programs is removed. Second, the work is real: through Launchpad Inc., a nonprofit social enterprise, participants build and ship deployed AI systems for Philadelphia organizations, so graduates finish with a portfolio and client references, not just a certificate. Third, Launchpad measures earning power over time toward a $50,000 living wage rather than a job on graduation day — an honest metric for the hardest-to-place, youngest entrants to the AI economy. The whole program runs against a versioned, openly licensed AI Engineer competency framework and is backed by Building 21's decade of competency-based education.

kb.partnerships.label: Partnerships
kb.partnerships.text: Launchpad works with {{employer_partners}} employer partners who inform the curriculum, host paid placements, sit on the advisory board, and run mock interviews and portfolio reviews — including Accenture (hosted the Cohort 1 graduation), Seer Interactive (hired a graduate over 200+ applicants, then more), Bentley Systems, CreateAccess (converted an intern to a permanent role), Hack Club, HiTouch Enterprises, AECOM, Nerd Street, PGW, and PECO. Through Launchpad Inc., participants have delivered paid client work for Philadelphia nonprofits and civic organizations including North10 Philadelphia, the Share Food Program, and Rock to the Future. Launchpad partners with Philadelphia high schools for recruitment, relies on parent organization Building 21 for the competency-based model and the Beacon platform, and has a dual-enrollment partnership with Mastery Charter School. A standing committee of industry professionals shapes the curriculum to what employers hire for.

kb.staff_bios.label: Key staff qualifications
kb.staff_bios.text: Launchpad is led by Executive Director Dannyelle Austin (Founding ED; 15+ years in education and workforce development). The team is {{staff_count_ft}} full-time and {{staff_count_pt}} part-time staff (all W-2), and includes program directors, technical instructors, coaches, a career placement coordinator, and Launchpad Inc. software-delivery leadership. Building 21 adds shared services that do not sit in that headcount — instructional design, finance, compliance, and the Beacon platform team — and is led by Co-CEOs Chip Linehan and Laura Shubilla. Industry mentors and advisory-board members contribute regular in-kind time through portfolio reviews, mock interviews, and curriculum input; several first-cohort alumni have returned to mentor and recruit the next cohort.

kb.dei.label: DEI practices
kb.dei.text: Equity is the design. Launchpad recruits from non-selective Philadelphia high schools that do not offer computer science, requires no prior experience, and pays participants so access to a high-paying tech career does not depend on which school a student attended or whether they can afford to train unpaid. The service population is about {{demographics_black_brown}} Black or Brown, nearly {{demographics_low_income}} low-income, and {{demographics_frl}} free/reduced-lunch eligible. Launchpad built the Entrepreneurial Leadership pathway so students not initially drawn to software engineering — including many young women who do not see themselves in a coding-only program — reach the same AI skills, paid projects, and credentials. Reaching young women in software specifically remains an active recruitment focus.

kb.goals.label: Short- and long-term goals
kb.goals.text: Short-term, Launchpad aims to move each cohort through to paid work and climbing earnings toward the $50,000 living-wage target, and to mature Launchpad Inc. into a predictable, replicable earned-revenue engine (pricing, client pipeline, project sequencing) that reduces grant reliance. Long-term, Launchpad aims to spin out as its own 501(c)(3) and to prove the model — the AI Engineer competency framework plus the paid Launchpad Inc. bridge — is transferable to new cities and employer markets, while deepening twelve-month retention and placement outcomes.

kb.innovation.label: What is new/different + significance
kb.innovation.text: Launchpad's innovation is a paid on-ramp that produces working professionals rather than a class that ends at a job fair. First, the AI Engineer competency framework: rather than teaching tools that are obsolete within a year, Launchpad defined the durable capabilities of an AI builder as six competencies and 24 skills, staged Associate → AI Engineer, each assessed against a shipped portfolio artifact, not a test score. The framework is versioned (now in its fifth version), reviewed by a standing curriculum committee, and openly licensed for other programs to adopt. Second, paid work from day one through Launchpad Inc., a real social enterprise: participants deploy AI systems for Philadelphia organizations that could not otherwise afford them, producing the deployed work and client references early-career tech hiring now demands while removing the financial barrier. Third, an honest redefinition of success — earning power over time toward a $50,000 living wage — which lets programs serving the hardest-to-place populations show real progress instead of failing a metric built for a labor market that no longer exists. If proven at scale, the model is transferable to other cities and employer markets.

kb.theory_of_change.label: Theory of change & impact example
kb.theory_of_change.text: The logic: young people break into the AI economy when they can prove they have done the work, and they can only prove it if finishing is financially possible. Inputs — philanthropic and earned revenue, an instructional team and career coaches, the Beacon platform and the AI Engineer competency framework, {{employer_partners}} employer partners, and a pipeline of paid client projects through Launchpad Inc. Activities — recruit young adults from low-income Philadelphia neighborhoods, pay them from day one, train them against the framework, place them on real client projects, wrap the program in supports (meals, transportation, laptops, coaching, financial counseling), and connect them to employers. Outputs — each participant completes roughly {{client_work_hours}} of paid client work, earns industry certifications (Generative AI Foundations, PCEP), and finishes with a portfolio of deployed AI systems and client references assessed in Beacon. Outcomes — graduates enter and hold paid work, and their earning power rises toward a $50,000 living wage over the year after graduation. The load-bearing assumption is the paid bridge: without pay from day one, financial pressure breaks persistence before the outcomes appear. Two feedback loops reinforce the chain: alumni return to mentor and recruit, and paid client work generates revenue that helps fund the next cohort. Early evidence: {{placement_numerator}} of {{placement_denominator}} in Cohort 1 in paid work or training at six months, {{alumni_wages}} in documented alumni wages. [Confirm a real, consented student story before using in an application.]

kb.risk.label: Risks, challenges & mitigation
kb.risk.text: Principal risks: (1) participant persistence across a full-time program for low-income young adults — mitigated by pay-from-day-one, wraparound supports, and Career Success Coaching that continues into the first year of employment; (2) dependence on employer partners for placements — mitigated by a diversified network of {{employer_partners}} partners so no single employer is load-bearing; (3) the funding required to pay participant stipends — mitigated by a diversified base (foundation, individual, government, corporate, PA EITC) plus the growing earned-revenue and dual-enrollment streams designed to reduce grant reliance; and (4) maturing Launchpad Inc. into a predictable, replicable business (pricing, pipeline, project sequencing) — the explicit focus of current capacity-building efforts.

kb.capacity.label: Organizational capacity & past performance
kb.capacity.text: Launchpad is operated by Building 21, a Philadelphia nonprofit founded in 2013 that has run competency-based schools and programs across 20 states serving 10,000+ students, and that provides Launchpad with instructional design, finance, compliance, and the Beacon competency/workforce-tracking platform — infrastructure a standalone startup could not replicate. Launchpad itself has three-plus years of development and one complete graduate cohort behind it: LiftOff designed 2022, first cohort enrolled January 2023 and graduated October 2025; the AI Engineer competency framework has been through five versions refined against real cohorts and employer feedback; Launchpad Inc. launched in 2025 and books client work. Past performance to date: {{students_served}} students served, LiftOff Cohort 1 at {{placement_rate_6mo}} in paid work or training at six months, and {{alumni_wages}} in documented alumni wages.
